what: Reproducible record of the README demo: the commands, the real session they ran against, and what came out. README and demo GIF share these facts.

demo_session.description: A real finished Claude Code session on this machine: adding node-affinity scheduling to a backfill Job in a Helm chart, 53 turns.
demo_session.conclusion_excerpt_first_line: Restored and verified. Final state confirmed — the template diff is back to the intended affinity block, lint passes, and the test (with the equality assertion) passes.
demo_session.note: Session content belongs to its author; the demo card and GIF show it unmodified.

commands.result: 20 finished sessions for that directory (16 codex, 4 claude), newest first
166 426350 — the whole answer is in there, as JSONL
one-screen answer card: verbatim conclusion (transcript:164) plus evidence rows with path:line refs; 29 evidence rows total, the fullest rows shown on screen and the rest counted in the footer
same card plus unbury-answer.html written to the working directory: full transcript with #L<line> anchors; every card row deep-links to its turn

gif.mode: real sessions (UNBURY_DEMO_PROJECT pointed at the project directory above); the tape renders the bundled synthetic example sessions when no real sessions exist

limitations: Extraction is heuristic, not model-backed: the conclusion is the final substantive assistant message, quoted verbatim; heuristic extraction is what keeps unbury zero-config and offline.
Agent log formats are undocumented and change without notice; parsers are fixture-tested per dialect and degrade gracefully (unparseable lines are counted, not fatal).
A Codex session counts as finished after its rollout file has been quiescent for five minutes; an in-flight session is never carded.
The card shows the rows that fit; the footer counts what was skipped and the HTML view always carries the full evidence table.
